article_title: Applying a Partially Nested Regression Model to Evaluate the Impact of ASSISTments on Middle School Students' Math Achievement
citation: Huang, C.-W., Feng, M., & Li, L. (2025). Applying a partially nested regression model to evaluate the impact of ASSISTments on middle school students' math achievement. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: vPLC-augmented ASSISTments intervention with four-step formative assessment process
description: The intervention combines WPI's ASSISTments online math platform with a virtual professional learning community (vPLC) designed to enhance scalability, reducing travel and scheduling barriers especially for rural districts. Teachers participated in eight vPLC sessions focused on using ASSISTments reports to differentiate instruction, establish routines, and discuss student data. During implementation, teachers followed a four-step formative process: create standards-aligned math assignments, assist students through immediate feedback, assess class performance, and analyze answers together to address common errors and adjust instruction.
requirements: Teacher participation in the eight vPLC sessions and implementation of the four-step formative process (Heritage & Popham, 2013) as part of using ASSISTments.
constraints: The intervention targets grades 6 through 8 math; prior studies showed ASSISTments improves learning when paired with in-person coaching, and the vPLC was added to reduce travel and scheduling barriers.
target_learners: middle school math teachers, including those in rural districts
target_learning_goals: teachers' use of ASSISTments reports to differentiate instruction and adjust teaching
examples: The study was conducted in two cohorts (2022–23 and 2023–24) with 59 middle school teachers and 2,855 students across 36 schools in 24 states; 55% of students were eligible for free or reduced-price lunch and about half were in rural areas.
key_sources: Huang, C.-W., Feng, M., & Li, L. (2025). Applying a partially nested regression model to evaluate the impact of ASSISTments on middle school students' math achievement. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677665

article_title: Scaling Teachers' Professional Development for ASSISTments: Evaluation Final Report
citation: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., Huang, C.-W., Luttgen, K., Grady, J., Yang, S., Lavine, A., Collins, K., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments: Evaluation final report. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Virtual professional learning community (vPLC): eight 75-minute synchronous sessions with asynchronous Slack activities, facilitated by former teachers
description: The vPLC is a scalable professional learning model designed to support effective ASSISTments implementation, particularly in rural and underresourced settings. "Teachers participated in eight 75-minute virtual sessions, each preceded by thought-provoking asynchronous activities delivered via Slack", facilitated by two former middle school teachers using a facilitation guide. Sessions follow a consistent structure including icebreakers, a Story From the Field, breakout discussions in small groups, a Teachers' Lounge segment, and digital sticky-note reflections.
requirements: Treatment teachers were expected to attend at least seven of eight synchronous vPLC sessions held between September and February and to complete at least four of eight asynchronous activities on Slack.
constraints: The vPLC was designed for rural educators who often lack access to local PLCs or peer networks; an optional ninth and tenth session were provided.
target_learners: Rural middle school math teachers in grades 6-8
target_learning_goals: Effective use of ASSISTments, formative assessment practice, and data-driven instructional decision-making
examples: Session topics ranged from establishing high expectations for all learners and reading assignment reports to orchestrating class discussions around open response questions and student engagement and motivation.
key_sources: Feng, M., Li, L., Brezack, N., Huang, C.-W., Luttgen, K., Grady, J., Yang, S., Lavine, A., Collins, K., & Schneider, M. (2025). Scaling teachers' professional development for ASSISTments: Evaluation final report. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677852

article_title: Integrating Insights from Volitional Personality Change Interventions to Improve Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Mathias Allemand, Brent W. Roberts, Ulrich Trautwein. (2026). Integrating Insights from Volitional Personality Change Interventions to Improve Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10127-6
title: VPC theory of change: enduring trait change arises from interplay of top-down volitional strategies and bottom-up behavioral repetition
description: The review describes VPC interventions as resting on the assumption that "traits can be modified through two complementary pathways: top-down and bottom-up." Top-down processes involve goal setting, self-reflection, and motivational alignment; bottom-up processes rely on repeated enactment of trait-relevant behaviors and repertoire expansion that accumulate into trait change. Supporting frameworks include TESSERA, Behavioral Activation, Intentional Change theories, and the General (Common) Change Factors model, whose four mechanisms are discrepancy awareness, activating strengths and resources, targeting thoughts and feelings to achieve insight, and targeting behaviors to be practiced.
requirements: Sustained motivation to change is a prerequisite that remains critical throughout the change process
Behavioral practice with feedback from coaches or peers to stabilize change through habit formation and reinforcement
constraints: Participants in research on personality change goals are typically aged 18 or older
The number of studies on VPC remains too limited to examine differences in the effects of various intervention methods
target_learning_goals: persistence and transfer of intervention effects
examples: The review describes the General (Common) Change Factors model's four mechanisms, including actuating discrepancy awareness by contrasting actual with desired personality profiles
key_sources: Mathias Allemand, Brent W. Roberts, Ulrich Trautwein. (2026). Integrating Insights from Volitional Personality Change Interventions to Improve Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10127-6

article_title: The effectiveness of virtual reality training on knowledge, skills and attitudes of health care professionals and students in assessing and treating mental health disorders: a systematic review.
citation: Sten CW, Söderström K, Stensrud B, Nylund IB, Siqveland J. (2024). The effectiveness of virtual reality training on knowledge, skills and attitudes of health care professionals and students in assessing and treating mental health disorders: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05423-0
title: Classification of virtual patient training interventions into virtual standardized patient, interactive patient scenario, and virtual patient game designs
description: The review applies an updated classification of virtual patient interventions, based on Kononowicz et al. developed from Talbot et al.'s model, to categorize the VR training designs in the included studies. It distinguishes three designs: the virtual standardized patient, "a conversational agent that simulates clinical presentations for training purposes"; the interactive patient scenario, which "primarily uses text-based multimedia, enhanced with images and case histories"; and the virtual patient game using 3D avatars for clinical reasoning and team training. Four studies used VSPs, two IPS, and two VP games.
requirements: The classification requires expertise in VR systems and learning design; the review used advisers from VRINN, SIMInnlandet, and an experienced VP scholar to categorize interventions.
constraints: The VSP interventions classified in the review predate modern artificial intelligence but are considered conversational agents because they include an algorithm that answers questions.
target_learning_goals: mental health assessment and treatment skills
examples: In the review's Table 1, the eight included studies are each categorized as VSP, IPS, or VP game with their VR system, duration, comparison, and outcome measures.
key_sources: Sten CW, Söderström K, Stensrud B, Nylund IB, Siqveland J. (2024). The effectiveness of virtual reality training on knowledge, skills and attitudes of health care professionals and students in assessing and treating mental health disorders: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05423-0

article_title: Do virtual patients prepare medical students for the real world? Development and application of a framework to compare a virtual patient collection with population data.
citation: Urresti-Gundlach M., Tolks D., Kiessling C., Wagner-Menghin M., Härtl A., Hege I. (2017). Do virtual patients prepare medical students for the real world? Development and application of a framework to compare a virtual patient collection with population data. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1013-1
title: Four-category coding framework for assessing the real-world authenticity of virtual patient collections
description: The article develops a coding framework with four main categories — patient data, patient representation, diagnoses, and setting — to analyze how well a virtual patient collection represents a relevant patient population and how patients are represented as persons. Codes cover sex, age, sexual orientation, BMI, disability, occupation, cultural/migration aspects, substance use, naming, social context, direct speech, emotions, multimedia, ICD-10 diagnoses, onset, setting, and scenario closure. The authors state: "We developed a coding framework to analyze the VP collection that is provided to medical students in the interdisciplinary year at LMU Munich and evaluate (1) its authenticity compared to the German population and (2) how the patient is represented as a person."
requirements: Requires statistical data from a healthcare system or population registry for comparison
Requires access to the full VP scenarios for coding
constraints: The full coding schema, including examples and more detailed descriptions, is only available upon request
target_learning_goals: assessing authenticity and diversity of virtual patient collections
examples: Applied to 66 virtual patients in the internal medicine and surgery curriculum at LMU Munich
key_sources: Urresti-Gundlach M., Tolks D., Kiessling C., Wagner-Menghin M., Härtl A., Hege I. (2017). Do virtual patients prepare medical students for the real world? Development and application of a framework to compare a virtual patient collection with population data. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1013-1

citation: Urresti-Gundlach M., Tolks D., Kiessling C., Wagner-Menghin M., Härtl A., Hege I. (2017). Do virtual patients prepare medical students for the real world? Development and application of a framework to compare a virtual patient collection with population data. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1013-1
title: VP authors should be made aware of personalized patient representation and collection-level diversity without overwhelming learners
description: The article recommends raising awareness among VP authors concerning personalized representations of patients and the real-world authenticity of a VP collection, while balancing this against cognitive load for students. The authors suggest expanding existing VP creation guidelines to include tips about implementing a realistic VP collection in terms of patient and context diversity. As they state: "We suggest raising awareness among VP authors concerning personalized representations of patients without overwhelming their students."
requirements: VP creation guidelines or systems should incorporate diversity and personalization guidance
Authors need awareness of their own biases and experiences when creating VPs
constraints: Personalization should not overwhelm students with excessive complexity or cognitive load
target_learning_goals: creating authentic and diverse virtual patient scenarios
examples: The article suggests expanding guidelines such as those by Posel et al. and Begg to address collection-level diversity

article_title: Virtual Patient Simulations in Health Professions Education: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis by the Digital Health Education Collaboration.
citation: Kononowicz AA, Woodham LA, Edelbring S, Stathakarou N, Davies D, Saxena N, Tudor Car L, Carlstedt-Duke J, Car J, Zary N. (2019). Virtual Patient Simulations in Health Professions Education: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis by the Digital Health Education Collaboration. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/14676
title: Use virtual patients to complement rather than replace bedside and real-patient contact
description: The review positions virtual patients as a modality in which learners actively train clinical reasoning and critical thinking before bedside learning, warning against using the results to justify reduced bedside teaching. It states virtual patients "should not replace but complement contact with real patients", and can have greater impact where knowledge is combined with skills in problem solving when direct patient contact is not yet possible.
requirements: Integration alongside, not in place of, real patient contact and bedside teaching
constraints: The review warns against justifying diminished hours of bedside teaching, which was investigated in just 1 study and did not show positive outcomes
examples: The review found skills benefits concentrated in clinical reasoning and procedural skills, interpreted as value at applied, problem-solving levels rather than lower Bloom's taxonomy levels
key_sources: Kononowicz AA, Woodham LA, Edelbring S, Stathakarou N, Davies D, Saxena N, Tudor Car L, Carlstedt-Duke J, Car J, Zary N. (2019). article_title: A qualitative analysis of virtual patient descriptions in healthcare education based on a systematic literature review.
citation: Hege Inga, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Tolks Daniel, Edelbring Samuel, Kuehlmeyer Katja. (2016). A qualitative analysis of virtual patient descriptions in healthcare education based on a systematic literature review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0655-8
title: Five-category concept map of virtual patient descriptions in healthcare education
description: The article develops a concept map synthesizing how virtual patients are described in the healthcare education literature. Five main categories were developed inductively-deductively, "stemming from a Simulation-based model developed by Issenberg" and the authors' shared understanding of VPs; the categories represent the life-cycle and environment of a VP with three main actors: the patient, the teacher who creates a VP, and the learner who engages with a VP, plus the VP itself as learning activity and the curriculum as environment. The map visualizes concepts and relations using CMap software and is offered as a dynamic resource for educators and researchers.
requirements: A coding frame with categories, subcategories, indicators, examples from the data, and decision rules
constraints: Based on researchers' and educators' views in the literature; the authors state it is unclear to what extent this represents other perspectives, such as the learners'
Related search terms such as case-based learning were deliberately excluded, so additional concepts might be revealed when expanding to such terms
target_learning_goals: Understanding the concept space of virtual patients in healthcare education
examples: The authors extracted 185 VP descriptions from 375 educational articles published 1991 through 2014 and coded them with a frame whose subcategories were developed by subsumption, reaching saturation after coding 10% of the descriptions
key_sources: Hege Inga, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Tolks Daniel, Edelbring Samuel, Kuehlmeyer Katja. (2016). A qualitative analysis of virtual patient descriptions in healthcare education based on a systematic literature review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0655-8

article_title: A qualitative analysis of virtual patient descriptions in healthcare education based on a systematic literature review.
citation: Hege Inga, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Tolks Daniel, Edelbring Samuel, Kuehlmeyer Katja. (2016). A qualitative analysis of virtual patient descriptions in healthcare education based on a systematic literature review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0655-8
title: Involve patients more deeply in virtual patient development beyond providing multimedia material
description: The article recommends moving patients beyond their current role as donors of authentic material in VP development. Patients could act as reviewers or feedback-givers to ensure their perspective is adequately represented and valued, especially for VPs presenting a patient's perspective, where "a deeper inclusion of patients into the VP development seems indispensable". Future VP development and research should focus on including patients beyond multimedia elements and investigate effects on perceived authenticity and learner engagement.
requirements: Willingness of VP developers to involve patients as reviewers or feedback-givers rather than only as material sources
constraints: The article states this recommendation rests on the observation that patients are currently under-valued; effects on perceived authenticity and learner engagement are proposed research questions, not demonstrated findings
target_learning_goals: Authentic representation of the patient perspective in virtual patient scenarios
examples: The article suggests patients could act as reviewers or feedback-givers to ensure their perspective is adequately represented and valued in VP development
key_sources: Hege Inga, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Tolks Daniel, Edelbring Samuel, Kuehlmeyer Katja. (2016). A qualitative analysis of virtual patient descriptions in healthcare education based on a systematic literature review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0655-8

article_title: A qualitative analysis of virtual patient descriptions in healthcare education based on a systematic literature review.
citation: Hege Inga, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Tolks Daniel, Edelbring Samuel, Kuehlmeyer Katja. (2016). A qualitative analysis of virtual patient descriptions in healthcare education based on a systematic literature review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0655-8
title: Develop and share virtual patients collaboratively to lower creation effort and costs
description: The article describes collaborative development and exchangeability as approaches to lower the effort and production costs of virtual patients. Medical schools have undertaken efforts to collaboratively develop and use VPs, and approaches have focused on "the exchangeability of virtual patients"; the eViP project focused on exchangeability among different institutions and across VP systems. Educators would benefit from a sophisticated study investigating the multifaceted costs of VP creation, use, and maintenance depending on the underlying VP technology.
requirements: Institutional collaboration or sharing infrastructure for VP development and exchange
constraints: The article notes branching cases are more difficult to construct and more expensive compared with linear cases, a cost factor that sharing initiatives must address
target_learning_goals: Cost-effective creation and maintenance of virtual patient cases
examples: The group of Berman et al. implemented a model to collaboratively develop VPs and share infrastructure costs among institutions; the eViP project focused on exchangeability of virtual patients among institutions and across VP systems

article_title: The Effects of Pre-Reading and Sharing Mechanisms on Learning with the Use of Annotations
citation: Wu-Yuin Hwang & Guo-Liang Hsu. (2011). The Effects of Pre-reading and Sharing Mechanisms on Learning with the Use of Annotations. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://www.tojet.net/
title: VPEN Web-based multimedia annotation system with sharing mechanism
description: VPEN is "a multimedia Web annotation system developed by Hwang and Wang (2004)" supporting highlighting, underlining, text and sound-recording comments, and reading or sharing annotations. Annotation contents are stored in a Microsoft SQL server, and each annotation records its type and time so pre-class annotations can be identified. In this study VPEN served the Experiment and Control A classes for pre-reading and in-class annotation, with a sharing mechanism in phase 2 letting students view classmates' annotations.
requirements: Students need computer and Web access to use VPEN; some participants could not see annotations at home
constraints: The VPEN Session protection mechanism could log users out and lose annotations after long inactivity, which frustrated around 36 percent of participants
target_learning_goals: pre-reading preparation in a sixth-grade social course
making explicit and inexplicit annotations on learning materials
examples: The Experiment class pre-read with VPEN and shared annotations in phase 2, scoring M=86.2 on the post-test
key_sources: Wu-Yuin Hwang & Guo-Liang Hsu. (2011). The Effects of Pre-reading and Sharing Mechanisms on Learning with the Use of Annotations. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ932242

article_title: Ensuring Knowledge Transfer: The Critical Role of "What-If" Discussions in Virtual Patient Simulation.
citation: Li Zhien, Asoodar Maryam, Keulers Tom, Joosten-ten Brinke Desirée, Dolmans Diana. (2026). Ensuring Knowledge Transfer: The Critical Role of “What-If” Discussions in Virtual Patient Simulation. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2363
title: Embed virtual patients within an integrated sequence of role modelling, varied case practice, feedback, and structured reflection rather than using them as isolated cases
description: The article proposes that VPs be embedded in a structured instructional sequence: students first observe expert role modelling, then practice with varied authentic cases, then engage in structured “what-if” discussions comparing cases. The authors state that “transfer appears to emerge from the coordinated sequencing of modelling, practice, feedback, and structured reflection”, suggesting variability of practice alone may be insufficient to support transfer.
requirements: Expert role modelling demonstration to provide a framework for subsequent cases
Varied VP cases with differing surface features such as patient age, comorbidities, and clinical presentation
Structured “what-if” questions with a detailed discussion guide
constraints: The observed effects reflect the integrated design rather than any individual component, making it difficult to isolate the specific contribution of each element
The role modelling and discussion were facilitated by an expert educator with substantial domain and teaching expertise, which may limit transferability to settings with less experienced instructors
target_learning_goals: near and far transfer of learning to new patient cases
examples: In the study, students observed an expert demonstrate reasoning on a neck cancer case, practiced individually with VP Cases B or C, discussed “what-if” questions in pairs, then completed paper-based near transfer (Case D) and far transfer (Case E) tasks
key_sources: Li Zhien, Asoodar Maryam, Keulers Tom, Joosten-ten Brinke Desirée, Dolmans Diana. (2026). Ensuring Knowledge Transfer: The Critical Role of “What-If” Discussions in Virtual Patient Simulation. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2363

article_title: A virtual patient-based training program to enhance clinical decision-making competencies in general practice residents: mixed-methods study.
citation: Chen Yuanshuai, Jiang Leyi, Wu Lingyan, Gong Wenxin, Wu Jingni, Zhen Junhai, Tong Yuling, Guo Yi, Xu Zhijie. (2026). A virtual patient-based training program to enhance clinical decision-making competencies in general practice residents: mixed-methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09607-8
title: Weekly cycle pairing repeated VP case practice with in-person expert-facilitated debriefing workshops
description: The program followed "a consistent weekly cycle": two new VP cases released each Tuesday, completed independently with unlimited attempts and immediate automated feedback, followed by a facilitated 2-hour workshop each Monday in which two residents presented their clinical decision-making process and two attending physicians gave structured feedback. A senior GP faculty member guided "a reflective discussion that compared different diagnostic strategies". This created a continuous cycle of individual practice, peer learning, and expert feedback, addressing the known limits of standalone screen-based simulation such as uncorrected misconceptions and cognitive overload.
requirements: In-person expert debrief integrated after case completion
Residents presenting their reasoning with prepared slides and attending physicians providing structured expert commentary
constraints: Workshop quality depended on facilitators' teaching skill; some sessions were dominated by vocal participants or became simple case review rather than deep reflective discussion
target_learning_goals: Clinical decision-making and diagnostic reasoning competencies
examples: Case pairs were chosen as complementary presentations (e.g., chest pain and dyspnea) or contrasting diagnostic challenges (e.g., acute vs. chronic headache)
key_sources: Chen Yuanshuai, Jiang Leyi, Wu Lingyan, Gong Wenxin, Wu Jingni, Zhen Junhai, Tong Yuling, Guo Yi, Xu Zhijie. (2026). A virtual patient-based training program to enhance clinical decision-making competencies in general practice residents: mixed-methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09607-8

article_title: A virtual patient-based training program to enhance clinical decision-making competencies in general practice residents: mixed-methods study.
citation: Chen Yuanshuai, Jiang Leyi, Wu Lingyan, Gong Wenxin, Wu Jingni, Zhen Junhai, Tong Yuling, Guo Yi, Xu Zhijie. (2026). A virtual patient-based training program to enhance clinical decision-making competencies in general practice residents: mixed-methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09607-8
title: Integrate VP training early in residency and wrap it in facilitated feedback, reflection, and peer dialogue, since the platform alone is necessary but insufficient
description: The article recommends treating VP platforms as one component of a pedagogically wrapped curriculum rather than standalone tools. It states "the VP platform alone is a necessary but insufficient component" and that "its educational power depends on the surrounding pedagogical wrap‑around, including feedback, reflection, and peer dialogue". The curriculum delivered the greatest benefit for first-year residents, suggesting VP training "works best when introduced early in residency, before clinical experience solidifies automatic reasoning". Facilitator training in structured debriefing methods is recommended to address variable workshop quality.
requirements: Weekly facilitated debriefing with trained facilitators and strategies ensuring equitable participation
Early introduction in the residency before automatic reasoning patterns consolidate
constraints: Single-group pre-post design precludes definitive causal attribution; benefits did not distribute evenly across training years, with third-year residents showing minimal changes
target_learners: First- and second-year general practice residents
target_learning_goals: Clinical decision-making, diagnostic reasoning, and management planning competencies
examples: The study integrated VP training into the standard residency curriculum for the entire 50-resident cohort over 12 weeks
key_sources: Chen Yuanshuai, Jiang Leyi, Wu Lingyan, Gong Wenxin, Wu Jingni, Zhen Junhai, Tong Yuling, Guo Yi, Xu Zhijie. (2026). A virtual patient-based training program to enhance clinical decision-making competencies in general practice residents: mixed-methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09607-8

article_title: The effect of AI-enabled virtual patient simulation on training outcomes and insecurities in psychotherapy education.
citation: Cecil Julia, Kokje Eesha, Kleine Anne-Kathrin, Schaffernak Insa, Vogel Lea, Angerer Selina, Lermer Eva, Gaube Susanne. (2026). The effect of AI-enabled virtual patient simulation on training outcomes and insecurities in psychotherapy education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09917-x
title: Use VP simulations with pre-briefings and enhanced authenticity as a scalable complementary method in psychotherapy training
description: The article concludes that AI-enabled virtual patient simulations can serve as a complementary training method alongside traditional formats. The authors state: "Design recommendations emphasize pre-briefings and enhancing VP authenticity to use VP simulations as a scalable, engaging complementary method in psychotherapy training." The recommendation is grounded in the finding that VP training improved competence and self-efficacy and reduced insecurity, while not exceeding video training, positioning VP as an addition rather than a replacement.
requirements: Pre-briefings before VP sessions (instructional video explaining platform navigation and the diagnostic task)
Enhanced VP authenticity to improve perceived realism
constraints: Effects did not surpass video training, so VP is positioned as complementary rather than superior
Knowledge about mental disorders was not enhanced by VP training
examples: Participants completed four interactive AI-enabled VP sessions on consecutive days, each featuring a different patient with depression, panic disorder, GAD, or adjustment disorder, with automated Motivational Interviewing feedback after each session.

The effect of AI-enabled virtual patient simulation on training outcomes and insecurities in psychotherapy education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09917-x

article_title: Reducing misdiagnoses and cognitive errors using virtual patients and automated feedback in a clinical reasoning curriculum.
citation: Waechter Jason, Kusnoor Anita, Eickman Kara, Smith David, Wong Matt, Rogers Suzanne, Lee Chel Hee. (2026). Reducing misdiagnoses and cognitive errors using virtual patients and automated feedback in a clinical reasoning curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08647-4
title: Deliberate-practice virtual patient case sequence with staged differential diagnosis revision and per-case feedback
description: A reusable curricular pattern in which learners complete common-disease virtual patient cases at regular intervals (every 3–4 weeks), each structured in four stages with iterative differential diagnosis creation and revision, active assignment of pertinent positives and negatives, and test results revealed only for ordered tests. "This iterative cycle of practice and feedback constituted deliberate practice", with automated scoring informing individualized feedback and a one-hour whole-class think-aloud review after each case. Case order strived for 25% overlap with the current organ system and 75% with previously taught systems.
requirements: Feedback, repetition, and sufficient case variety
Automated scoring to minimize faculty workload
Cases with typical presentations of common diagnoses
constraints: Did not assess information gathering through history-taking or physical examination
Simulated setting; translation to real-life clinical environments remains unclear
target_learners: Pre-clerkship medical students in large cohorts
target_learning_goals: Diagnostic accuracy and diagnostic clinical reasoning components
examples: 23 cases with typical presentations covering 58 diagnoses across 15 systems/categories; cases equally spaced throughout pre-clerkship
key_sources: Waechter Jason, Kusnoor Anita, Eickman Kara, Smith David, Wong Matt, Rogers Suzanne, Lee Chel Hee. (2026). Reducing misdiagnoses and cognitive errors using virtual patients and automated feedback in a clinical reasoning curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08647-4

article_title: Development and validation of virtual patients for assessing history taking and communication skills among medical students.
citation: Mohd Salim Nurul Ain, Azman Azreen, Sulaiman Puteri Suhaiza, Roslan Nurhanis Syazni, Hod Rafidah, Adam Siti Khadijah. (2026). Development and validation of virtual patients for assessing history taking and communication skills among medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08503-x
title: Fidelity spectrum of virtual patients, from text-based low-fidelity cases to AI-enhanced high-fidelity immersive simulations
description: The article organizes virtual patients along a spectrum of "levels of fidelity, interactivity, and realism, from simple, text-based formats to complex, AI-enhanced environments". Low-fidelity VPs rely on text-based cases, decision-tree models or rule-based systems with limited interactivity and serve foundational learning such as case-based learning and early clinical reasoning. High-fidelity VPs incorporate AI, natural language processing, speech recognition and physiological modeling for dynamic, realistic experiences, exemplified by the Oxford Medical Simulation VR package. The present system sits at the high-fidelity end, integrating voice-enabled communication through the Syn Bot framework with immersive 3D consultation environments.
requirements: High-fidelity operation requires AI, NLP and speech-recognition technologies and substantial software development and avatar-modeling resources
constraints: The article notes VPs may not yet capture the full complexity, responsiveness and interactive depth of real-time human SPs
examples: The article cites the Oxford Medical Simulation used at Hull York Medical School as a high-fidelity VR-based example
key_sources: Mohd Salim Nurul Ain, Azman Azreen, Sulaiman Puteri Suhaiza, Roslan Nurhanis Syazni, Hod Rafidah, Adam Siti Khadijah. (2026). Development and validation of virtual patients for assessing history taking and communication skills among medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08503-x

article_title: Virtual patient simulation strengthens confidence in clinical conversations among undergraduated nursing students: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Sörman K, El Alaoui S, Mårtensson S, Larsson M, Knez R, Ljudvåg M, Mac R, Dahlström K, Nowak YE, Fors U, Eckerström J. (2025). Virtual patient simulation strengthens confidence in clinical conversations among undergraduated nursing students: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08413-y
title: Interactive virtual patient simulation module on intimate partner violence (VCS platform)
description: A virtual patient case built on the Virtual Case System platform featuring a 41-year-old fictional patient named Sarah presenting with sleep disturbances, anxiety and depressive symptoms, with pre-recorded video clips of a professional actor. The simulation has five components: background information, a conversation interface, completed rating scales (GAD-7, PHQ-9, AUDIT), a written assessment section, and feedback in which questions are "graded as inappropriate (−1), neutral (0) or appropriate (+ 1)". Each session lasted 30 to 60 minutes.
requirements: Used after a web-based IPV course and followed by a teacher-led seminar as part of a three-part module
constraints: Developed for psychiatric education with a focus on IPV; evaluated in a single-site exploratory trial with N = 54
target_learning_goals: recognising, addressing and reflecting on intimate partner violence in clinical conversations
examples: In the RCT, the intervention group completed the VP module in addition to the standard curriculum while controls received standard training only, with crossover access granted after follow-up
key_sources: Sörman K, El Alaoui S, Mårtensson S, Larsson M, Knez R, Ljudvåg M, Mac R, Dahlström K, Nowak YE, Fors U, Eckerström J. (2025). Virtual patient simulation strengthens confidence in clinical conversations among undergraduated nursing students: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08413-y

article_title: Virtual patient simulation strengthens confidence in clinical conversations among undergraduated nursing students: a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Sörman K, El Alaoui S, Mårtensson S, Larsson M, Knez R, Ljudvåg M, Mac R, Dahlström K, Nowak YE, Fors U, Eckerström J. (2025). Virtual patient simulation strengthens confidence in clinical conversations among undergraduated nursing students: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08413-y
title: Integrate interactive virtual patient simulations into health-professions curricula as a complement to conventional teaching for complex and sensitive clinical topics
description: The article concludes that integrating an interactive VP simulation into a nursing curriculum enhances learners' confidence in addressing IPV and is associated with higher factual knowledge, positioning "VP simulations may represent a scalable complement to conventional teaching for complex and sensitive clinical topics". The VP provides safe practice of difficult patient conversations with structured expert feedback, which the authors link to the added confidence benefit.
requirements: Embedding within an existing curriculum alongside web-based education and a reflective teacher-led seminar
constraints: Evidence base is a small, single-site, exploratory RCT with a short follow-up; the authors call for replication in larger and more diverse cohorts
target_learning_goals: confidence and factual knowledge for sensitive clinical conversations, such as intimate partner violence inquiry
examples: The trial added a 30–60 minute VP session on IPV to the fourth-semester nursing course at the University of Skövde, with control students granted access after follow-up for ethical reasons
key_sources: Sörman K, El Alaoui S, Mårtensson S, Larsson M, Knez R, Ljudvåg M, Mac R, Dahlström K, Nowak YE, Fors U, Eckerström J. (2025). Virtual patient simulation strengthens confidence in clinical conversations among undergraduated nursing students: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08413-y

article_title: Bridging the gap to clinical practice: a concept for virtual patients in preclinical education in prosthetic dentistry.
citation: Schulz Marco S., Pantelmann Ragna, Hillebrecht Anna-Lena, Reissmann Daniel R. (2025). Bridging the gap to clinical practice: a concept for virtual patients in preclinical education in prosthetic dentistry. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08097-4
title: Virtual-patient e-learning tool with three prosthodontic cases on the CASUS platform
description: An e-learning tool built on the online platform CASUS® presenting three patient cases documented by dentists, covering a single crown in the maxilla, crowns and conventional bridges, and complete/partial denture rehabilitation. Cases and exercises of varying difficulty were included so the tool offered relevant content for students with different prior knowledge without individual customization. Patient dialogues were filmed and documentation such as x-rays was used to make the environment realistic. The tool emphasized both clinical knowledge and soft skills through case-based tasks.
requirements: Internet access and students' access to required hardware; the platform was tested on multiple devices and browsers
constraints: Developed and evaluated exclusively in the context of prosthodontic cases; voluntary use meant not all participants used it
target_learners: third- and fourth-year dental students in preclinical prosthetic dentistry
target_learning_goals: psychosocial, interdisciplinary, organizational and dental competences for comprehensive dental treatment
examples: Cases were created on CASUS® (Instruct AG, Munich, Germany), which has a linear structure and supports a wide variety of media and task types
key_sources: Schulz Marco S., Pantelmann Ragna, Hillebrecht Anna-Lena, Reissmann Daniel R. (2025). Bridging the gap to clinical practice: a concept for virtual patients in preclinical education in prosthetic dentistry. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08097-4

article_title: Virtual Patients Using Large Language Models: Scalable, Contextualized Simulation of Clinician-Patient Dialogue With Feedback.
citation: Coristine A, Li D, Foroutan DB, Ojo TF, Menon NP, Aditya I, Cook DA, Overgaard J, Pankratz VS, Del Fiol G, Aakre CA. (2025). Virtual Patients Using Large Language Models: Scalable, Contextualized Simulation of Clinician-Patient Dialogue With Feedback. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/68486
title: Three-instrument framework for rating VP dialogue authenticity, user experience, and feedback quality
description: The authors developed and validated three novel rating instruments grounded in literature on dialogue systems, natural language generation, VP authenticity frameworks, presence, and feedback research. Dialogue authenticity items capture responses that are "humanlike," "coherent," "personal," and "relevant"; user experience items capture realness, cognitive authenticity, variability, and involvement; feedback items capture evidence-based observations, actionable suggestions, connected observations-and-suggestions, and balanced praise and critique. A validation study collected content, internal structure, relations-with-other-variables, and response-process evidence.
requirements: Expert review (3 experts in VPs or natural language generation approved the instruments) and operational criteria for response options
constraints: Reproducibility was suboptimal: authenticity/experience ICCs 0.17-0.40 (fair) and feedback ICCs mostly ≤0.17 (slight)
examples: Used to rate 60 conversations by 3 blinded physicians and GPT, with mixed models ANOVA for subgroup comparisons
key_sources: Coristine A, Li D, Foroutan DB, Ojo TF, Menon NP, Aditya I, Cook DA, Overgaard J, Pankratz VS, Del Fiol G, Aakre CA. (2025). Virtual Patients Using Large Language Models: Scalable, Contextualized Simulation of Clinician-Patient Dialogue With Feedback. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/68486

article_title: Virtual patients versus standardized patients for improving clinical reasoning skills in ophthalmology residents. A randomized controlled trial.
citation: Malik Tayyaba Gul, Mahboob Usman, Khan Rehan Ahmed, Alam Rabia. (2024). Virtual patients versus standardized patients for improving clinical reasoning skills in ophthalmology residents. A randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05241-4
title: Use virtual patients as a safe, repeatable alternative to standardized patients when repeated practice is needed, since SP availability limits repetition
description: The article recommends VPs where trainees need repeated patient encounters that real patients cannot safely provide and that standardized patients cannot sustain logistically. In the trial's words, "VPs can be used for learning clinical reasoning skills in postgraduate ophthalmology residents in a safe environment" and can be "used repeatedly without any risk to the real patient", while "SP is limited by its nonavailability for repeated exercises". This principle applies to clinical reasoning practice, not to interpersonal skill training.
requirements: VP cases must be specialty specific and validated for the domain; the article emphasizes that "It is important to emphasize that VPs are specialty specific."
constraints: VPs cannot teach bedside manners, patient welfare or communication skills, per the article's stated limitation.
The evidence base in ophthalmology is thin: the article states "much work needs to be done in Ophthalmology, for which little evidence is available."
target_learners: Postgraduate medical residents, particularly in specialties with limited patient availability for repeated encounters
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning and diagnostic decision-making skills
examples: In the trial, VP and SP groups received the same cases and equivalent 30-minute exercises, with the VP group achieving statistically indistinguishable posttest and follow-up performance.
key_sources: Malik Tayyaba Gul, Mahboob Usman, Khan Rehan Ahmed, Alam Rabia. (2024). Virtual patients versus standardized patients for improving clinical reasoning skills in ophthalmology residents. A randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05241-4

article_title: Planning a Collection of Virtual Patients to Train Clinical Reasoning: A Blueprint Representative of the European Population.
citation: Mayer Anja, Da Silva Domingues Vital, Hege Inga, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Larrosa Marcos, Martínez-Jarreta Begoña, Rodriguez-Molina Daloha, Sousa-Pinto Bernardo, Sudacka Małgorzata, Morin Luc. (2022). Planning a Collection of Virtual Patients to Train Clinical Reasoning: A Blueprint Representative of the European Population. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19106175
title: Four-category taxonomy of blueprint criteria: disease-, patient-, learner- and encounter-related
description: The article organizes the variables specified for every VP into four categories. Disease-related criteria cover final diagnoses, key symptoms, disease onset, and scenario closure; patient-related criteria cover demographic and identity characteristics; learner-related criteria cover the learner's role in the scenario; encounter-related criteria cover the consultation setting. The authors grouped criteria "into (i) disease-related, (ii) patient-related, (iii) learner-related, and (iv) encounter-related criteria" and mapped diagnoses to MeSH and national competency frameworks to ease curricular integration. The taxonomy operationalizes situativity theory's claim that clinical reasoning depends on contextual factors related to the patient and the encounter.
requirements: Permitted values defined for each criterion and a template allowing partners to populate the blueprint with VP data
constraints: The article states no European data sources based on patient populations were available for comparison, so general-population statistics were used instead
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning, diagnostic decision-making, awareness of contextual factors and biases
examples: Table 1 lists criteria and permitted values, e.g., setting values of Rural Hospital, University Hospital, Hospital, Practice, Outpatient Clinic, and Emergency Room
key_sources: Mayer Anja, Da Silva Domingues Vital, Hege Inga, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Larrosa Marcos, Martínez-Jarreta Begoña, Rodriguez-Molina Daloha, Sousa-Pinto Bernardo, Sudacka Małgorzata, Morin Luc. (2022). Planning a Collection of Virtual Patients to Train Clinical Reasoning: A Blueprint Representative of the European Population. article_title: Adaptation of an international virtual patient collection to the COVID-19 pandemic.
citation: Hege I, Sudacka M, Kononowicz AA, Nonnenmann J, Banholzer J, Schelling J, Adler M, Espinoza B, Garrido MA, Radon K. (2020). Adaptation of an international virtual patient collection to the COVID-19 pandemic. GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(7): Doc92. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7740015/
title: Use virtual patients as a valuable addition to bedside teaching for safe-environment clinical reasoning practice, not as a replacement
description: The authors recommend integrating VP collections into curricula even when face-to-face teaching with patients is possible again, "not as a replacement for bedside teaching, but as a valuable addition for training in a safe environment". They argue VPs allow medical schools to document achieving required learning objectives related to clinical presentations when patient contacts are hindered, and support deliberate practice of clinical reasoning.
requirements: Integration into curricula alongside, rather than instead of, face-to-face patient contact
constraints: The recommendation is framed for medical education contexts where bedside teaching with patients remains available
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning practice in a safe environment; documenting learning objectives related to clinical presentations
examples: During the pandemic, VPs gave medical schools a way to document required clinical-presentation learning objectives that were impossible to reach otherwise.
key_sources: Hege I, Sudacka M, Kononowicz AA, Nonnenmann J, Banholzer J, Schelling J, Adler M, Espinoza B, Garrido MA, Radon K. (2020). Adaptation of an international virtual patient collection to the COVID-19 pandemic. GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(7): Doc92. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7740015/

article_title: Codeveloping a Virtual Patient Simulation to Foster Nurses' Relational Skills Consistent With Motivational Interviewing: A Situation of Antiretroviral Therapy Nonadherence.
citation: Rouleau G, Pelletier J, Côté J, Gagnon M-P, Martel-Laferrière V, Lévesque R, SimforHealth, Fontaine G. (2020). Codeveloping a Virtual Patient Simulation to Foster Nurses’ Relational Skills Consistent With Motivational Interviewing: A Situation of Antiretroviral Therapy Nonadherence. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/18225
title: Virtual patient simulation on the MedicActiV platform for nurse-patient consultation in antiretroviral therapy nonadherence
description: The VP simulation depicts Mr Wilson, a 50-year-old man living with HIV whose viral load is "over 1000 copies/ml" after a treatment change and disrupted routine. Clinical content comprises a prebriefing video and text, the virtual nurse-patient consultation with the patient's electronic record, a web-based glossary, quizzes with feedback loops, and green and red visual labels. It is hosted on MedicActiV, a software-as-a-service platform with an authoring tool, and uses a 2D interface with 3D content considered nonimmersive virtual reality.
requirements: A prebriefing establishes standardized MI information and a fiction contract before the consultation.
constraints: The clinical case was embedded in a research process and available only to a small sample of research participants, not to all platform users.
target_learning_goals: relational skills consistent with motivational interviewing in nonadherence situations
examples: Green and red labels qualify the nurse's speech during the automated dialogue, corresponding to theoretical MI techniques and limiting the number of pathways to be scripted.
key_sources: Rouleau G, Pelletier J, Côté J, Gagnon M-P, Martel-Laferrière V, Lévesque R, SimforHealth, Fontaine G. (2020). Codeveloping a Virtual Patient Simulation to Foster Nurses’ Relational Skills Consistent With Motivational Interviewing: A Situation of Antiretroviral Therapy Nonadherence. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/18225

article_title: Virtual patients as a tool for training pre-registration pharmacists and increasing their preparedness to practice: A qualitative study.
citation: Thompson Jessica; White Simon; Chapman Stephen. (2020). Virtual patients as a tool for training pre-registration pharmacists and increasing their preparedness to practice: A qualitative study. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0238226
title: Use virtual patient simulations to let pre-registration trainees practise realistic scenarios in a safe environment and bridge training variation
description: The article recommends VPs as a novel training tool giving learners the opportunity to practise realistic scenarios in a safe environment. Trainees valued that "you make a mistake in the simulation you haven't killed anyone and you can try again", and the authors conclude VPs "offer the potential to 'bridge the gap' in pharmacist pre-registration sector-related training variation". Reported uses include individual revision, group learning, OSCE preparation, competency evidence, and replacing role-plays with a tutor.
requirements: Cases grounded in up-to-date, evidence-based guidelines and designed to pre-defined learning objectives
Web-based delivery allowing access anywhere with an internet connection
constraints: VPs may add little value when learners are working at lower levels of Bloom's taxonomy; the article suggests they should be used when knowledge is combined with skills in problem-solving scenarios or when direct patient contact is not possible
target_learning_goals: applying knowledge in realistic clinical scenarios
examples: Trainees reported using VPs as replacements for role-plays with a tutor, feeling more relaxed than when being watched
All trainees reported they would use the learning tools in future, most commonly for Continuing Professional Development
key_sources: Thompson Jessica; White Simon; Chapman Stephen. (2020). Virtual patients as a tool for training pre-registration pharmacists and increasing their preparedness to practice: A qualitative study. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0238226

article_title: Design and implementation of virtual patients for learning of clinical reasoning.
citation: Huwendiek S. (2019). Design and implementation of virtual patients for learning of clinical reasoning. GMS Journal for Medical Education 36(4):Doc33. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001241.shtml
title: Virtual Patient typology: 19 factors across four categories (general, educational, instructional design, technical)
description: The article presents a Virtual Patient typology developed from the literature, a review of existing VP systems, results from a student focus-group study, and an international modified-Delphi consensus among VP experts. It "synthesised 19 factors concerning four categories identified as relevant to VP design", giving researchers and designers a common reference point for studies or reports on Virtual Patients. The typology organises VP design attributes from general metadata to technical integration.
requirements: Development drew on the literature, a review of existing VP systems, results from the student focus-group study, and an international consensus process among Virtual Patient experts applying a modified Delphi technique
examples: The expert team consisted of all six authors of the paper; factors range from title, description and typical study time to path type, media use, feedback use, originating system and format.
key_sources: Huwendiek S. (2019). Design and implementation of virtual patients for learning of clinical reasoning. GMS Journal for Medical Education 36(4):Doc33. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001241.shtml

article_title: Design and implementation of virtual patients for learning of clinical reasoning.
citation: Huwendiek S. (2019). Design and implementation of virtual patients for learning of clinical reasoning. GMS Journal for Medical Education 36(4):Doc33. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001241.shtml
title: Short VP design questionnaire with one global score and six questions across three factors, validated with 2547 student evaluations of 78 Virtual Patients
description: A validated instrument to evaluate Virtual Patient design from the student perspective. It "comprises one global score and six questions distributed between three factors: authenticity of patient encounter and consultation, cognitive strategies in the consultation, coaching during consultation." Validity evidence covered content, response process and internal structure; an exploratory factor analysis of 2547 student evaluations of 78 VPs from three countries yielded a three-factor model with reasonable fit.
requirements: To reliably evaluate a Virtual Patient on all three factors, a minimum of 200 student responses are required
target_learning_goals: evaluation of virtual patient design for clinical reasoning learning
examples: Think-aloud studies and analysis of free-text comments supported the questionnaire's validity; nine VP experts from the eVIP project supported the content analysis.
key_sources: Huwendiek S. (2019). Design and implementation of virtual patients for learning of clinical reasoning. GMS Journal for Medical Education 36(4):Doc33. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001241.shtml

article_title: Design and implementation of virtual patients for learning of clinical reasoning.
citation: Huwendiek S. (2019). Design and implementation of virtual patients for learning of clinical reasoning. GMS Journal for Medical Education 36(4):Doc33. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001241.shtml
title: Sequencing Virtual Patients and other educational activities according to complexity, aligned with instruction and assessment
description: A curriculum-level pattern for embedding VPs in a clerkship: VPs and other activities, including bedside teaching with real patients, are sequenced according to complexity, and instruction and assessment are aligned with VP use. The article reports that studies 4–5 suggest "sequencing VPs and other educational activities, including bedside teaching with real patients, according to complexity" and "aligning instruction and assessment with the use of VPs". Students proposed a concrete sequence of lecture, one to two VPs, tutor-led small group discussion, then a real patient.
requirements: Continuous and stable online access; VP-related workload offset by elimination of other activities
constraints: Findings derive from student perceptions in one paediatric clerkship setting; no longitudinal implementation study was included
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clinical clerkships
examples: Students deemed optimal sequencing important, e.g. lecture – 1 to 2 VP(s) – tutor-led small group discussion – real patient, and wanted VP topics included in assessment.
key_sources: Huwendiek S. (2019). Design and implementation of virtual patients for learning of clinical reasoning. GMS Journal for Medical Education 36(4):Doc33. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001241.shtml

article_title: Design and implementation of virtual patients for learning of clinical reasoning.
citation: Huwendiek S. (2019). Design and implementation of virtual patients for learning of clinical reasoning. GMS Journal for Medical Education 36(4):Doc33. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001241.shtml
title: Design Virtual Patients using instructional design criteria — appropriate difficulty, authenticity, interactivity, feedback and focus on relevant learning points — and embed virtual coaching on clinical reasoning
description: The article recommends optimising VP design through instructional design criteria and embedded virtual coaching. Studies 1–3 suggest three main aspects: "use of instructional design criteria, i.e. ensuring appropriate difficulty, authenticity, interactivity, feedback and focus on relevant learning points", "implementation of virtual coaching on clinical reasoning into the VP, i.e. asking for discriminating and confirming features", and provision of validated instruments for systematic improvement. Well-designed VPs left students feeling very well prepared for reasoning in real patients.
requirements: Validated instruments such as the VP typology and VP design questionnaire to enable systematic further improvements
constraints: The questionnaire provides valid information contingent on a large number of responses per VP; three studies were done at only one centre
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clinical clerkships
examples: In study 1, fifth-year students exposed to at least eight VPs discussed VP design in focus groups, yielding ten design principles including virtual coaching elements such as asking for discriminating and confirming features.
key_sources: Huwendiek S. (2019). Design and implementation of virtual patients for learning of clinical reasoning. GMS Journal for Medical Education 36(4):Doc33. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001241.shtml

article_title: The virtual patient as a learning tool: a mixed quantitative qualitative study.
citation: Isaza-Restrepo Andrés, Gómez María Teresa, Cifuentes Gary, Argüello Arturo. (2018). The virtual patient as a learning tool: a mixed quantitative qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1395-8
title: Use virtual patients within a constructivist environment with feedback, repetition, and integration — not as a standalone replacement
description: The authors conclude that "a learning environment that promotes individual construction through peer interaction, meaningful learning, repetition of the same problem with different variations, learning by doing and a proper permanent feedback are essential to ensuring the efficacy of a Web-based virtual patient". They also agree that simulation success depends not on simulation accuracy but on how it is used by instructor and student, and that the VP cannot completely replace other teaching strategies.
requirements: Feedback, repetition, curriculum integration, individualized learning and a controlled environment, as the article cites as conditions for effective simulation
constraints: The article states the VP is insufficient to simulate the complexity of the physician-patient interaction and complementary methodologies must be used
examples: The elective course combined VP cases with small group question-guided discussions and professor guidance; participants evidenced the need for videos, mock patients, and visits from advanced peers
key_sources: Isaza-Restrepo Andrés, Gómez María Teresa, Cifuentes Gary, Argüello Arturo. (2018). The virtual patient as a learning tool: a mixed quantitative qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1395-8

article_title: Uncovering the relation between clinical reasoning and diagnostic accuracy - An analysis of learner's clinical reasoning processes in virtual patients.
citation: Hege I, Kononowicz AA, Kiesewetter J, Foster-Johnson L. (2018). Uncovering the relation between clinical reasoning and diagnostic accuracy – An analysis of learner's clinical reasoning processes in virtual patients. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0204900
title: A concept mapping tool combined with virtual patients that documents, scores and gives feedback on the clinical reasoning process
description: The tool attaches to web-based virtual patients and lets learners document their clinical reasoning by adding nodes in four categories—"problems/findings, differential diagnoses they want to consider, tests they would like to perform ... and treatment options"—plus a summary statement, connected to show relationships. It automatically detects errors such as premature closure, scores nodes against expert maps using MeSH-based synonym matching, scores summary statements on semantic qualifiers, and stores all interactions. In this study it served both as a learning scaffold and as a research instrument measuring 1,393 reasoning processes.
requirements: Learners must submit a final diagnosis to conclude a scenario, and the system requires expert concept maps per VP, a MeSH synonym list and an adapted semantic-qualifier rubric for automatic scoring
constraints: Nodes already visible in the consulted expert map are scored as zero, which the authors state kept overall scores quite low; connections between nodes were rarely used, possibly due to a usability issue or need for more instruction
examples: 67 German and 30 English VPs in the CASUS system were offered free to students from January 1st until July 31, 2017 with registration required; 317 users completed at least one VP
key_sources: Hege I, Kononowicz AA, Kiesewetter J, Foster-Johnson L. (2018). Uncovering the relation between clinical reasoning and diagnostic accuracy – An analysis of learner's clinical reasoning processes in virtual patients. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0204900

article_title: Learning through a virtual patient vs. recorded lecture: a comparison of knowledge retention in a trauma case.
citation: Courteille Olivier, Fahlstedt Madelen, Ho Johnson, Hedman Leif, Fors Uno, von Holst Hans, Felländer-Tsai Li, Möller Hans. (2018). Learning through a virtual patient vs. recorded lecture: a comparison of knowledge retention in a trauma case. International Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.5aa3.ccf2
title: Virtual Patient spinal trauma case with interactive history-taking, examination, testing, SBAR reporting and summative feedback
description: A VP-based learning component built on a cervical spine trauma case from a motorcycle accident. Participants "act as the doctor assessing the patient at an emergency unit", ask medical-history questions of varying relevance, examine the patient, order laboratory or imaging tests, view the biomechanical simulations interactively, make a diagnosis, report via the SBAR tool, discuss treatment options, and receive summative feedback on all actions. Sessions averaged 45 minutes.
requirements: Participants work through the case individually on a computer, completing history, examination, testing, diagnosis and SBAR reporting before receiving summative feedback
constraints: The study evaluated trainee performance in only one patient case, which the authors state presumably would have affected outcomes if broader
target_learning_goals: assessment, diagnosis and treatment of spinal trauma
examples: In the trial, participants completed the VP session individually in about 45 minutes, ending with summative feedback based on all actions and decisions
key_sources: Courteille Olivier, Fahlstedt Madelen, Ho Johnson, Hedman Leif, Fors Uno, von Holst Hans, Felländer-Tsai Li, Möller Hans. (2018). Learning through a virtual patient vs. recorded lecture: a comparison of knowledge retention in a trauma case. International Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.5aa3.ccf2

article_title: Training with virtual patients in transcultural psychiatry: do the learners actually learn?
citation: Pantziaras I, Fors U, Ekblad S. (2015). Training With Virtual Patients in Transcultural Psychiatry: Do the Learners Actually Learn? Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3497
title: Virtual patient model combining experiential learning with automated theoretical feedback
description: The article proposes a virtual patient design model in which experiential learning, "as presented by Kolb", through active training in a realistic and appealing virtual environment is "enhanced by short theoretical frameworks integrated into automated feedback". The virtual patient encounter serves as the experiential core, while the individualized feedback module supplies the theoretical grounding tied to the learner's performance. The authors report that their results support this combination for acquiring core knowledge alongside clinical reasoning and decision-making skills.
requirements: a realistic and appealing virtual environment
short theoretical frameworks integrated into automated feedback
constraints: It has been suggested that VPs are not an ideal methodology for facilitating core knowledge, given potential cognitive overload and the fact that less interactive methods might be more effective
target_learning_goals: acquisition of core knowledge about PTSD
examples: The RT-SIM feedback module gives the patient's perspective of the consultation while a virtual advisor addresses PTSD diagnostic criteria, clinical management, and communication skills
key_sources: Pantziaras I, Fors U, Ekblad S. (2015). Training With Virtual Patients in Transcultural Psychiatry: Do the Learners Actually Learn? Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.3497

article_title: Design and evaluation of a simulation for pediatric dentistry in virtual worlds.
citation: Papadopoulos L, Pentzou A-E, Louloudiadis K, Tsiatsos T-K. (2013). Design and Evaluation of a Simulation for Pediatric Dentistry in Virtual Worlds. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.2651
title: Use virtual-world virtual patients as a supplement to, not a replacement for, traditional teaching methods
description: The article positions virtual-world simulations as additive to lecture-based teaching: the Erietta simulation supplemented the pediatric dentistry course's lectures, and the authors state that "these new methods of creating educational material are intended to support the traditional learning methods, not to replace them". The measured knowledge gain occurred in a supplement condition, so the recommendation is bounded by that design.
requirements: Existing traditional instruction (e.g., a lecture-based course covering the same techniques) for the simulation to supplement
constraints: The study tested supplementation only; replacement was not evaluated
target_learning_goals: knowledge of pediatric behavior and communication management techniques
examples: The experimental group received the simulation in addition to the lecture-based Pediatric Dentistry course already completed by all participants
key_sources: Papadopoulos L, Pentzou A-E, Louloudiadis K, Tsiatsos T-K. (2013). Design and Evaluation of a Simulation for Pediatric Dentistry in Virtual Worlds. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.2651

article_title: Virtual patients in primary care: developing a reusable model that fosters reflective practice and clinical reasoning.
citation: Helena Salminen, Nabil Zary, Karin Björklund, Eva Toth-Pal, Charlotte Leanderson. (2014). Virtual Patients in Primary Care: Developing a Reusable Model That Fosters Reflective Practice and Clinical Reasoning. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.2616
title: VP primary care model: iterated Kolb-inspired learning cycles embedding reflection-in-action and clinical reasoning
description: The article's core model is a virtual patient design for primary care in which each learning cycle contains a didactic inventory, a concrete multimedia experience, preformulated teacher feedback, and the student's free-text reflection, with iterated cycles inspired by Kolb's experiential learning. The authors state that "The iterated self-regulated learning cycles, one of the essential parts of the VP model were inspired by Kolb’s learning cycle", mapping doing, observing, thinking, and doing again onto planning, multimedia experience, reflection after feedback, and text revision. Reflection-in-action is embedded in every cycle and ends with a reflection-on-action, exposing students' clinical reasoning.
requirements: A VP system allowing open-ended questions, free-text answers, and video clips
Preformulated teacher comments (100–250 words) preceding students' reflective writing in each part
constraints: The reflective writing step takes time, limiting the number of cycles that can be inserted
No synchronous interaction between student and tutor in the chosen prototype system
target_learners: medical students in primary care placements

title: Five-cycle VP structure aligned with an authentic patient consultation
description: The VP case is organized as five iterated cycles mirroring the phases of a real primary care consultation. The article states: "The VP model was designed and divided into five cycles in alignment with an authentic patient consultation: Gathering information, Physical examination, Preliminary diagnosis, Explanation and planning, and Closing session". Each cycle pairs a student task and free-text answers with a video or material of the encounter, preformulated feedback, and student reflection; students begin by formulating learning goals and end with a final reflection.

Alignment of case learning outcomes with the study program's learning objectives
constraints: Five cycles took about 1.5 hours, which the authors regard as a time limit for an effective learning activity

citation: Georg C, Zary N. (2014). Web-Based Virtual Patients in Nursing Education: Development and Validation of Theory-Anchored Design and Activity Models. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.2556
title: Virtual patient Nursing Design Model (vpNDM): a three-layer theory-anchored blueprint for authoring VPs in nursing education
description: The vpNDM is a design blueprint grounded in the 3rd-generation nursing process (OPT model) that specifies what elements a VP for nursing education should contain. As the article states, "A virtual patient Nursing Design Model (vpNDM) composed of three layers was developed." Layer 1 covers patient-centric data collection (patient story, interviews, physical examination, observation, measurement scales, records), Layer 2 covers iterative clinical reasoning (framing, cue logic, juxtaposing, testing, judgment), and Layer 3 covers measurable outcomes such as data analysis, documentation, prioritizing interventions, and reflection. It is intended as a guideline for teachers authoring VPs.
requirements: Requires contextualization in an educational setting with specific intended learning and/or assessment outcomes
constraints: The authors acknowledge that "a model could hide the complexity of people's health care needs" requiring collective competence of different professions, and that contextualized models should be revisited for other health care professions
examples: Two VP cases were authored from the model: a woman in her 40s with rheumatoid arthritis-related chronic pain, and an older man with type 2 diabetes, heart failure, and an acute diabetic foot.

title: Virtual patient Nursing Activity Model (vpNAM): translating the design model into a VP-centric learning activity
description: The vpNAM is an activity model that combines the vpNDM with a specific educational context and intended learning outcomes, reinforcing that "VPs are not merely an object/tool but rather a learning activity." As the article states, "A virtual patient Nursing Activity Model (vpNAM) was also developed as a guide when creating VP-centric learning activities." When applied, the student is introduced to the patient and activity aims, collects relevant data to frame the patient's story and needs, and afterwards receives formative feedback formulated in advance by the case author, which the student uses to reflect and identify further learning needs. It was illustrated in the third semester of the undergraduate nursing program at Karolinska Institutet.
requirements: Requires intended learning outcomes and defined learning goals from the course plan to inform the modeling process
examples: The vpNAM was applied to a second-year undergraduate nursing course, with goals based on the nursing process, nursing documentation, and nursing diagnosis.
